p.src: Now, when Uncle He the Ninth fell to the ground, the undertaker’s men caught and supported him. Granny Wang cried, “He has been struck by an evil influence! Bring water, quickly!” After they sprayed two mouthfuls over him, Uncle He slowly began to move and somewhat recovered consciousness. Granny Wang said, “Help Uncle Nine home for now; we shall deal with matters afterward.” Two of the undertaker’s men used a removable door panel as a stretcher and carried Uncle He straight home. His whole household received him, and he lay down upon the bed. His wife wept, “You went out smiling and cheerful—how have you come home like this? Never before did I know you to be struck by an evil influence.” She sat beside the bed and sobbed. Seeing that the undertaker’s men were no longer nearby, Uncle He nudged his wife with his foot and said, “Do not fret. There is nothing wrong with me. Just now, as I was going to prepare Wu the Elder for burial, I reached the mouth of his lane and met Ximen Qing, who keeps the medicine shop by the county offices. He invited me to a banquet, gave me ten taels of silver, and said, ‘Whatever you find upon the corpse you are to encoffin, kindly cover it up.’ When I reached Wu the Elder’s house, I saw that his wife was a wicked woman. I was already eight or nine parts suspicious. When I lifted the funerary streamer and looked, Wu the Elder’s face was purplish black, blood was slowly seeping from all seven apertures, and faint tooth marks showed upon his lips. He had certainly died of poison. I meant to raise an outcry, but feared that, with no one to champion him, offending Ximen Qing would be no better than stirring up hornets and scorpions. Yet if I muddle through and encoffin him without question, Wu the Elder has a brother—the Constable Wu who slew the tiger on Jingyang Ridge the other day—and he is a man who kills without blinking. If he should return sooner or later, this affair will surely come to light.”

p.src: His wife replied, “I too heard someone say the other day, ‘Yunge, old Qiao’s son from the rear lane, went to Purple Stone Street to help Wu the Elder catch the adulterers and caused an uproar in the teahouse.’ That must be the very affair. You should quietly seek him out and question him. There is nothing difficult about the matter now. Have the undertaker’s men encoffin him themselves, and ask when the funeral will take place. If they keep the coffin at home until Wu Song returns to conduct the burial, there will be no tangled mystery in it. Even if they take him out and bury him at once, that too need cause no concern. But if they mean to take him out and burn him at once, there must be something suspicious. When the time comes, merely go as though to attend the funeral. While no one is looking, take two pieces of bone and keep them with these ten taels of silver. Together they will make powerful evidence. If he returns and asks no questions, let the matter rest. You will have spared Ximen Qing’s reputation, and it would be wrong not to preserve a livelihood for yourself.”

p.src: Uncle He said, “A worthy wife at home sees matters with perfect clarity.” He immediately summoned the undertaker’s men and instructed them: “I have been struck by an evil influence and cannot go. You must encoffin him yourselves. Ask when the funeral will take place, and hurry back to report. Divide among yourselves whatever money or cloth you receive, and see that everything is properly done. If they offer anything for me, do not accept it.” The men obeyed and went to Wu the Elder’s house. When they had encoffined him, laid out the coffin, and installed the spirit tablet, they returned and reported to Uncle He: “The mistress of the house said, ‘In just three days we shall take him out for burial and cremate him beyond the city.’” The men divided the money among themselves and dispersed. Uncle He said to his wife, “What you said was exactly right. When the day comes, I need only go and steal some of the bones.”

p.src: Meanwhile, Granny Wang urged everything forward with all her might, and that woman kept vigil beside the spirit that night. On the second day she engaged four monks to chant scriptures. Early on the third day, the undertaker’s men came of their own accord to shoulder the coffin, and several neighbors from the street accompanied the procession. The woman donned mourning dress and feigned tears all along the road to keep up appearances before the household and neighbors. On reaching the cremation ground outside the city, she ordered them to kindle the fire and burn the corpse. Just then Uncle He the Ninth appeared, carrying a string’s worth of paper money. When he entered the grounds, Granny Wang and the woman greeted him, saying, “Uncle Nine, how fortunate that you have recovered.” Uncle He said, “The other day I bought a tray of joined steamed cakes from the elder brother and never paid him. I have specially brought this string of paper money to burn for him.” Granny Wang said, “Uncle Nine, you are truly sincere.” After burning the paper money, Uncle He urged them to burn the coffin. Granny Wang and the woman thanked him: “It is good of Uncle He to take charge. When we return home, we shall thank you properly as well.” Uncle He replied, “Wherever I go, I merely lend a willing hand. Mistress and godmother, please make yourselves comfortable in the refectory and attend to all the neighbors. I shall look after matters here for you.” Having sent the woman and the old crone away, he took fire tongs, selected two pieces of bone, and dipped them briefly into the bone-washing pool. The bones proved brittle and black. Uncle He hid them away, then went to the refectory and joined the company for a while. When the coffin had burned through, the cremation attendants gathered up the remains and rinsed them in the pool. The assembled neighbors then went their separate ways. Uncle He took the bones home, wrote the year, month, and day and the names of those who had attended the funeral upon a sheet of paper, wrapped it together with the silver, placed everything in a cloth bag, and stored it in his room.

p.src: As for the woman, after returning home she set up a spirit tablet before the lattice partition, inscribed: “Seat of My Late Husband, Wu the Elder.” Before the spirit couch she lit a glass lamp and arranged scripture banners, stacks of paper money, paper ingots of gold and silver, colored silks, and similar offerings. Yet every day she and Ximen Qing amused themselves upstairs as they pleased. It was no longer like their former furtive, illicit pleasures in Granny Wang’s room: now there was no one in the house to offend their eyes, and they could remain in bed together all night at will. From then on, Ximen Qing would remain away from his own home for three or five nights at a stretch, and everyone in his household, high and low, was displeased. p.src: As the saying goes, “At the height of joy sorrow is born; when adversity reaches its limit, prosperity returns.” Time flew swiftly, and before long more than forty days had passed. After Wu Song had received the magistrate’s orders, he escorted the convoy to the magistrate’s relative in the Eastern Capital, delivered the letter, and handed over the chests and baggage. He spent several days strolling through the streets, obtained a letter of reply, and then led his party back along the road to Yanggu County. The outward and return journeys together had taken almost exactly two months. When he left, it was the weather of early spring; when he returned, the third month had just begun. All along the road he felt uneasy in spirit and distracted in body and mind, and he hastened back, eager to see his elder brother. First he went to the county offices and delivered the reply. The magistrate was overjoyed to see him. After reading the reply and learning that all the gold, silver, valuables, and goods had been properly delivered, the magistrate rewarded Wu Song with a large ingot of silver and entertained him with wine and food, as goes without saying.

p.src: Wu Song said, “Please stop, sister-in-law. Do not weep! When did my brother die? What illness did he have? Whose medicine did he take?” Weeping as she spoke, the woman said, “Some ten or twenty days after you left, your brother was suddenly stricken with a violent pain in his heart. He was ill for eight or nine days. We prayed to the gods, consulted diviners, and tried every kind of medicine, but nothing could cure him, and he died. He has left me to suffer so bitterly!” Granny Wang next door heard this and, fearing the truth might come out, hurried over to help her cover the matter up. Wu Song asked again, “My brother never suffered from such an illness before. How could a pain in the heart have killed him?” Granny Wang said, “Captain, how can you speak so? ‘The heavens bring unforeseeable storms, and men meet sudden fortune or calamity.’ Who can be sure of remaining forever unharmed?” The woman said, “I owe everything to this godmother of mine. I am like a crab without legs, helpless on my own. If not for my godmother here, which of the neighbors would have been willing to help me?” Wu Song asked, “Where is he buried now?” The woman replied, “I was all alone. Where could I have gone to find a burial plot? There was nothing else to be done, so I kept him for three days, then had him carried out and cremated.” Wu Song asked, “How many days has my brother been dead?” The woman replied, “In two more days it will be the end of the seventh seven-day mourning period.”

p.src: The woman opened the door, and Wu Song told the soldier to prepare soup and rice. Before the memorial altar, Wu Song lit the lamps and candles and set out wine and food. By the second watch everything had been properly arranged. Wu Song threw himself down in worship and said, “Brother, may your spirit not be far away! You were meek while alive, and now that you are dead, the truth of your fate has not come to light. If you suffered injustice and died with a grievance, murdered by another’s hand, appear to me in a dream; your brother will uphold your cause and avenge you.” He poured out the wine as a libation, burned the spirit money, and burst into loud weeping. His weeping made all the neighbors on either side grieve with him. Inside, the woman also pretended to weep. When Wu Song had finished weeping, he ate the soup, rice, wine, and food with the soldier, then asked for two mats and told the soldier to sleep beside the middle door. Wu Song took one mat and slept before the memorial altar. The woman went upstairs, barred the stair door, and slept by herself.

p.src: At about the third watch, Wu Song tossed and turned, unable to sleep. When he looked at the soldier, the man lay stretched out like a corpse, snoring loudly. Wu Song scrambled up and looked at the glass lamp before the memorial altar; its flame flickered between light and darkness. He listened closely to the watch drum: it was sounding the third beat of the third watch. Wu Song sighed, sat upon the mat, and said to himself, “My brother was timid while alive; now that he is dead, how could he make the truth known?” Before he had finished speaking, a gust of cold air rose from beneath the memorial altar—truly, it swirled with bone-piercing cold and cut through the flesh with bitter chill. Dim and murky, the lamplight before the spirit tablet lost its glow; dismal and eerie, the paper money on the walls flew wildly about. The cold blast made every hair on Wu Song’s body stand on end. Peering intently, he saw a man crawl out from beneath the memorial altar and cry, “Brother, how bitterly I died!” Wu Song could not see him clearly. Just as he was about to step forward and question him again, the cold air dispersed and the figure vanished. Wu Song toppled backward onto the mat and sat there, wondering whether it had been a dream or not. When he turned to look at the soldier, the man was fast asleep. Wu Song thought, “There must certainly be something unexplained about my brother’s death. …Just now he meant to tell me the truth, but the force of my vital spirit scattered his soul. …” He kept the matter in his heart and said no more, waiting until daybreak to investigate further. p.src: The sky gradually brightened, and the soldier rose to heat water. Wu Song washed and rinsed his mouth. The woman also came downstairs, looked at Wu Song, and said, “Were you troubled last night, brother-in-law?” Wu Song said, “Sister-in-law, what illness did my brother truly die of?” The woman replied, “How can you have forgotten, brother-in-law? He managed the entire removal.” Wu Song said, “So that is how it was. I shall first go to the county offices to answer the roll, then return.” He set off with the soldier. On reaching the entrance to Purple Stone Street, he asked, “Do you know Uncle He the Ninth, the head of the undertakers?” The soldier replied, “How can you have forgotten, Captain? He came before to offer congratulations to you. His house is just inside Lion Street.” Wu Song said, “Lead me there.” The soldier led Wu Song to Uncle He the Ninth’s door. Wu Song said, “You go on ahead.” The soldier departed. Wu Song raised the curtain and called, “Is Uncle He the Ninth at home?” Uncle He the Ninth had only just risen. Hearing that Wu Song had come looking for him, he was thrown into such confusion that he had no time even to put on his headcloth. He hurriedly took the silver and the bone fragments and hid them on his person, then came out to welcome him, saying, “When did you return, Captain?” Wu Song replied, “I returned here only yesterday. There is a small matter I should like to discuss with you. Please accompany me.” Uncle He the Ninth said, “I shall come at once. Please first honor me by taking some tea, Captain.” Wu Song said, “That will not be necessary. Spare yourself the trouble.”

p.src: When the magistrate saw them, he asked, “What complaint does the constable wish to bring?” Wu Song stated his charge: “My own elder brother, Wu Da, was murdered by Ximen Qing and my sister-in-law, who were committing adultery and poisoned him. These two men are witnesses. I beg Your Honor to see justice done.” The magistrate first questioned Uncle He Jiu and Yun'ge and took down their statements, then conferred that day with the county clerks. As it happened, all the county clerks had dealings with Ximen Qing, to say nothing of the magistrate himself. The officials therefore conspired together and concluded, “This case is difficult to adjudicate.” The magistrate said, “Wu Song, you are yourself a constable of this county. How can you be ignorant of the law? As the old saying goes: ‘To catch adulterers, find the pair together; to catch a thief, find the stolen goods; to prove murder, find the wounds.’ Your brother’s corpse is gone, and you did not catch the pair in the act; if we were to try them for murder solely on the words of these two men, would that not be showing excessive partiality? You must not act rashly. Think the matter over yourself, and act only when it is proper to do so.” Wu Song drew from inside his robe two pieces of charred black bone, ten taels of silver, and a sheet of paper, and pleaded, “I respectfully submit to Your Honor that these things were surely not fabricated by me.” After examining them, the magistrate said, “Rise for now and let me consider the matter at length. If action can be taken, I shall have the accused arrested and questioned for you.” Wu Song kept both Uncle He Jiu and Yun'ge in his quarters. That same day Ximen Qing learned of the matter and sent a trusted agent to the county offices to promise silver to the officials. Early the next morning, Wu Song petitioned in the court and pressed the magistrate to make arrests. But who would have thought that the official, coveting the bribe, would return the bones and silver and say, “Wu Song, do not listen to outsiders inciting you to make an enemy of Ximen Qing. This affair is unclear and cannot readily be brought to trial. The Sage said: ‘Even what one has seen with one’s own eyes may not be true; how then can one wholly trust words spoken behind another’s back?’ You must not act rashly in the heat of the moment.” A prison clerk added, “Constable, in every homicide case there must be a corpse, wounds, a cause of death, physical evidence, and traces—the case can be investigated only when all five are present.” Wu Song said, “Since Your Honor will not admit my complaint, I shall pursue the matter in another way.” He took back the silver and bones and again entrusted them to Uncle He Jiu for safekeeping. Leaving the court, he returned to his own quarters and ordered the soldiers to prepare a meal for Uncle He Jiu and Yun'ge. “Stay here and wait for a while. I shall be back soon.”

p.src: Taking another two or three constables with him, he left the county offices, bringing an inkstone, brushes, and ink, then bought several sheets of paper and concealed them on his person. He told two constables to buy a pig's head, a goose, a chicken, a shoulder-pole load of wine, and some fruit and other provisions, and have them prepared at the house. At about the hour of the Snake, he brought the constables home. The woman already knew that her accusation had been rejected. Her mind at ease and no longer afraid of him, she boldly waited to see what he would do. Wu Song called, “Sister-in-law, come downstairs. I have something to say.” The woman slowly came downstairs and asked, “What do you have to say?” Wu Song said, “Tomorrow marks the end of the seventh seven-day mourning period for my late brother. The other day you offended all our neighbors, so today I have come especially to offer them wine and apologize on your behalf.” The woman said haughtily, “What is there to thank them for?” Wu Song replied, “Courtesy must be observed.” He first ordered the constables to go before the spirit couch, light two bright candles and a censer of incense, lay out a string of spirit money, and arrange the offerings before the altar, heaping the dishes high and setting out wine, food, fruit, and the like. He told one constable to warm the wine in the rear; two constables to arrange tables and stools by the front door; and another two to guard the front and rear doors. When Wu Song had given all his orders, he said, “Sister-in-law, attend to the guests while I go invite them.” First he invited Granny Wang from next door. The old woman said, “You need not put yourself to such trouble and offer me thanks, Captain.” Wu Song said, “I have imposed greatly upon you, godmother, and have my reasons for doing this. I have prepared a humble cup of wine and a few dishes, so please make no excuses.” The old woman took down her shop sign, secured the premises, and came around through the back door. Wu Song said, “Sister-in-law, take the place of honor, and godmother, sit opposite her.” The old woman already knew that Ximen Qing had sent back word, so she drank with an easy mind. Both women thought, “Let us see what he means to do.” Wu Song next invited Yao Erlang, Yao Wenqing, who kept the silversmith's shop on the other adjoining side. Erlang said, “I am rather busy. There is no need for you to trouble yourself, Captain.” Wu Song caught hold of him and said, “It is only a cup of plain wine and will not take long. Please come to the house.” Yao Erlang had no choice but to comply and come along, and he was seated below Granny Wang. Then Wu Song went across the street to invite two households—one was Zhao Silang, Zhao Zhongming, who kept a shop selling paper funeral offerings. Silang said, “I cannot leave my business unattended, so I am unable to join you.” Wu Song said, “How could that do? All our good neighbors are already there.” Giving him no choice but to come, Wu Song dragged him to the house and said, “You, venerable sir, are like a father to us. Please sit below my sister-in-law.” He also invited Hu Zhengqing, who sold chilled wine across the street. The man had once been a clerk in the yamen and immediately sensed something awkward about the affair, so he was quite unwilling to come; but Wu Song paid no heed and dragged him over, then seated him below Zhao Silang. Wu Song asked, “Granny Wang, who lives next door to you?” Granny Wang replied, “That is Old Zhang, who sells filled dough dumplings.” As luck would have it, the old man was at home. Seeing Wu Song enter, he started and said, “Captain, is something the matter?” Wu Song said, “Our household has often troubled the neighbors, so I have come to invite you for a cup of plain wine.” The old man exclaimed, “Goodness! I have never paid my respects at your house, Captain. How then could you invite me to drink?” Wu Song said, “It is but a trifling token of respect. Please come to the house.” The old man was dragged over by Wu Song and seated below Yao Erlang.

Giving him no choice but to come, Wu Song dragged him to the house and said, “You, venerable sir, are like a father to us. Please sit below my sister-in-law.”
He also invited Hu Zhengqing, who sold chilled wine across the street.
The man had once been a clerk in the yamen and immediately sensed something awkward about the affair, so he was quite unwilling to come;
but Wu Song paid no heed and dragged him over, then seated him below Zhao Silang.
Wu Song asked, “Granny Wang, who lives next door to you?”
Granny Wang replied, “That is Old Zhang, who sells filled dough dumplings.”
As luck would have it, the old man was at home. Seeing Wu Song enter, he started and said, “Captain, is something the matter?”
Wu Song said, “Our household has often troubled the neighbors, so I have come to invite you for a cup of plain wine.”
The old man exclaimed, “Goodness!
I have never paid my respects at your house, Captain. How then could you invite me to drink?”
Wu Song said, “It is but a trifling token of respect. Please come to the house.”
The old man was dragged over by Wu Song and seated below Yao Erlang.

p.src: Now Wu Song had invited four neighboring households, and with Granny Wang and his sister-in-law there were six guests in all. Wu Song brought over a stool and sat at the end of the table, then ordered the constables to shut the front and rear doors. The constable in the rear came forward as usual to pour the wine. Wu Song made a deep bow and said, “Good neighbors, please forgive my rough manners and the haphazard nature of my invitation.” The neighbors said, “We have never even held a welcoming feast to wash away the dust of your journey, Captain, yet now we have come to impose upon you instead.” Wu Song smiled. “It is scarcely worthy of mention. Good neighbors, please do not laugh at my poor offering.” The constable kept pouring wine. Everyone harbored anxious suspicions, quite unable to tell what was afoot. When they had drunk about three cups, Hu Zhengqing rose to leave, saying, “I have some business to attend to.” Wu Song shouted, “You cannot go! Since you have come, sit awhile even if you are busy.” Hu Zhengqing's heart was like fifteen buckets drawing water from a well, seven going up and eight coming down. He thought uneasily, “If he invited us to drink out of goodwill, why treat us like this and forbid anyone to leave?” He had no choice but to sit down again. Wu Song said, “Pour more wine.” The constable poured a fourth round; after the seven cups they had drunk altogether, the guests felt as if they had endured a thousand banquets given by Empress Lü. Then Wu Song shouted to the constables to clear away the cups and dishes for the time being, saying they would drink again presently. Wu Song wiped the table clean. Just as the neighbors were about to rise, Wu Song barred their way with both hands and said, “There is something I wish to discuss. Of all the good neighbors gathered here, which one can write?” Yao Erlang said, “Hu Zhengqing here writes exceedingly well.” Wu Song bowed and said, “May I trouble you, then?” He rolled up both sleeves, reached beneath his clothes, and with a swish drew out that sharp knife. Curling the four fingers of his right hand around the hilt and pressing his thumb against the guard, he opened his fierce, round eyes wide and said, “Good neighbors, you are all gathered here. Every wrong has its perpetrator, and every debt its debtor. I ask only that you bear witness.”

p.src: Wu Song seized his sister-in-law with his left hand and pointed at Granny Wang with his right. The four neighbors stared open-mouthed in terror, utterly at a loss; they looked from one to another and dared not utter a sound. Wu Song said, “Good neighbors, do not blame me, and do not be alarmed. Though Wu Song is a rough fellow who does not fear even death, he still understands that a wrong must be avenged upon the one who committed it and a feud upon its proper enemy. I will do none of you any harm; I ask only that you serve as witnesses. But if any one of you tries to leave first, do not blame Wu Song for turning upon him. I shall let him taste five or seven thrusts of my knife, and this Second Brother Wu will gladly pay for it with his own life.” All the neighbors stood staring in speechless terror and did not dare move again.

p.src: Wu Song glared at Granny Wang and shouted, “Listen well, you old swine!” “My brother’s death lies entirely at your door. I shall question you at my leisure!” Then he turned to the woman and cursed her: “Listen, you adulterous wretch!” “Tell me truthfully how you plotted to murder my brother, and I will spare you.” The woman said, “Brother-in-law, how unreasonable you are!” “Your brother died of his own heart ailment. What has that to do with me?” Before she could finish, Wu Song drove the hilt of his knife into the table, seized her topknot with his left hand, and gripped the front of her dress with his right. He kicked the table over, effortlessly hauled the woman across it, flung her down before the spirit couch, and pinned her beneath his feet; then, drawing the knife with his right hand, he pointed it at Granny Wang and said, “Old swine, tell the truth!” The old woman tried to escape but could not, so she said, “There is no need for the constable to be angry. This old woman will tell you everything.” Wu Song ordered the soldiers to bring paper, ink, brush, and inkstone and arrange them on the table. Pointing his knife at Hu Zhengqing, he said, “I must trouble you to listen and write down every sentence.” Trembling all over, Hu Zhengqing said, “I—I shall write it.” He asked for some water for the inkstone and ground the ink. Then Hu Zhengqing took up the brush, spread the paper, and said, “Granny Wang, tell the truth!” The old woman said, “It has nothing to do with me. What would you have me say?” Wu Song said, “Old swine, I know everything already. Whom do you think you can deceive?” “If you refuse to speak, I shall first carve up this adulterous wretch and then kill you, old cur.” He raised the knife and made two slashes toward the woman’s face. The woman cried out in terror, “Brother-in-law, spare me for the moment!” “Let me get up, and I shall tell you.” With one tug Wu Song hauled the woman up and made her kneel before the spirit couch. Wu Song roared, “Speak quickly, you adulterous wretch!”

p.src: The woman was frightened out of her wits and had no choice but to confess everything truthfully: how she had dropped the blind and struck Ximen Qing, how clothes had been made, and how they had begun their adulterous affair—she related it all, detail by detail. She went on to recount how Wu Da had later been kicked, why they had devised the poisoning, and how Granny Wang had incited and directed them, telling the whole story from beginning to end. For every sentence she spoke, Wu Song had Hu Zhengqing write down a sentence. Granny Wang said, “You biting little vermin! Now that you have confessed first, how can I deny it? You have brought misery upon this old woman!” Granny Wang, too, had no choice but to confess. Wu Song also had Hu Zhengqing write down the old woman’s deposition. Everything from beginning to end was recorded there. He made both women set their fingerprints and marks upon it, then had the neighbors from the four adjoining households sign their names and add their marks as well. He ordered a soldier to remove his waist sash and bind the old cur’s arms behind her back, then rolled up the depositions and concealed them inside his robe. He told a soldier to fetch a bowl of wine and set it as an offering before the spirit couch. Then he dragged the woman over and made her kneel before the spirit, and shouted at the old woman to kneel there too. Wu Song said, “Brother, may your spirit be near! Your younger brother, Wu the Second, shall avenge your death and wipe away your grievance!” He ordered a soldier to set the spirit money alight. Seeing that matters had taken an ominous turn, the woman was about to cry out, but Wu Song seized her by the hair and threw her down. He planted his feet upon her arms and tore open the clothes over her breast; and quicker than words can tell, he plunged the sharp knife once into her chest, gripped the blade between his teeth, tore her breast open with both hands, and ripped out her heart, liver, and entrails as an offering before the spirit. With one slicing stroke he cut off the woman’s head, and blood flowed all over the floor. The neighbors from the four households were horrified and covered their faces. Seeing how fierce he was, they dared not move and could only comply with him. Wu Song ordered a soldier to bring down a quilt from upstairs. He wrapped the woman’s head in it, wiped his knife, sheathed it, washed his hands, and bowed, saying, “I have put my good neighbors to much trouble; please forgive me.” “Please sit upstairs for a while. Wu the Second will return shortly.” The neighbors from the four households looked at one another. None dared disobey him, so they all went upstairs and sat down. Wu Song instructed the soldiers to escort the old woman upstairs as well. He shut the upper-story door and stationed two soldiers below to keep watch.

p.src: Having wrapped up the woman’s head, Wu Song went straight to the front of Ximen Qing’s apothecary shop. He bowed to the manager and asked, “Is the master here?” The manager said, “He has just gone out.” Wu Song said, “Step aside with me. I have a private word to say.” The manager recognized Wu Song to some extent and dared not refuse to come out. Wu Song led him into a secluded side alley. Wu Song wheeled around and said, “Do you want to die, or do you want to live?” The manager said in alarm, “Honored constable, I have never done you any injury or offense.” Wu Song said, “If you want to die, say nothing of Ximen Qing’s whereabouts;” “but if you want to live, tell me truthfully where Ximen Qing is.” The manager said, “He just went—with an acquaintance—to drink—upstairs at the great tavern—by Lion Bridge.” On hearing this, Wu Song turned and left at once. The manager stood terrified for a long while, unable to move his feet, before finally going on his way.

p.src: Now Wu Song hurried straight to the tavern by Lion Bridge and asked a waiter, “With whom is Master Ximen Qing drinking?” The waiter said, “With another wealthy gentleman of his sort, in a private room upstairs overlooking the street.” Wu Song charged straight upstairs. Peering toward the private room, he saw through the window opening that Ximen Qing occupied the host’s seat, another man sat opposite in the guest’s place, and two singing girls were seated on either side. Wu Song opened the quilt bundle and gave it a shake. The blood-soaked human head rolled out. Holding the head in his left hand and drawing the sharp knife with his right, Wu Song flicked aside the curtain and burst inside, hurling the woman’s head straight into Ximen Qing’s face. Ximen Qing recognized Wu Song and cried in alarm, “Aiya!” He sprang onto a stool, planted one foot upon the windowsill, and sought a way to escape. But seeing the street below and that he could not jump down, he panicked. Quicker than words can tell, Wu Song pressed down lightly with one hand and, with a thump, leapt onto the table, kicking all the cups and dishes to the floor. The two singing girls were too frightened to move. The wealthy gentleman floundered in panic and also fell over in fright. Seeing Wu Song’s ferocious advance, Ximen Qing feinted with one hand and swiftly lashed out with his right foot. Wu Song, intent only on charging in, saw the kick coming and shifted slightly aside. The foot struck his right hand squarely, sending the knife flying out and down into the middle of the street. When Ximen Qing saw that he had kicked away the knife, he no longer feared Wu Song. He feinted with his right hand and drove his left fist toward Wu Song’s solar plexus. But Wu Song slipped aside, ducked beneath the blow, hooked his left arm around Ximen Qing’s head and shoulder and heaved upward, while his right hand seized Ximen Qing’s left leg. With a shout of “Down you go!” First, Ximen Qing was ensnared by the wronged spirit; second, Heaven’s justice would not suffer him; and third, how could he withstand Wu Song’s mighty strength? Head downward and feet in the air, he plunged upside down into the middle of the street and was knocked senseless—Chapter Eleven. The people on both sides of the street were all astounded.
